title: Systems & row reduction
description: Turn several equations into one clear path to a solution.
learningObjectives: Represent a system as an augmented matrix.
Explain why row operations preserve solutions.
Distinguish one, no, and infinitely many solutions.
bigIdea: A system asks for values that make every equation true at once. Think of two lines: their shared point is a solution. Elimination replaces equations with easier equivalent equations until the shared values become visible.

definitions.text: A linear equation uses unknowns only to the first power. The coefficients a and b and the constant c are fixed numbers.
An augmented matrix keeps the coefficients on the left and the constants on the right.
A pivot is the first nonzero entry in a nonzero row. In reduced row-echelon form each pivot is 1 and is the only nonzero entry in its column.

reasoning: Swapping equations does not change which values satisfy them. Multiplying an equation by a nonzero number is reversible. Adding a multiple of another equation is reversible by subtracting that multiple. Reversibility is why these operations preserve the entire solution set.

formulas.text: Allowed row operations; k must be nonzero in the scaling operation.
formulas.math: R_i\leftrightarrow R_j,\qquad R_i\leftarrow kR_i,\qquad R_i\leftarrow R_i+kR_j

steps.text: Write the two equations together.
Add the equations; y cancels because y + (−y) = 0.
Substitute x = 3 into the first equation and subtract 3.
Check both original equations.
Encode the coefficients and constants.
Subtract twice row 1 from row 2.
Divide row 2 by −5, then subtract twice row 2 from row 1.
Read the pivots as x = 3 and y = 2; check 3 + 4 = 7 and 6 − 2 = 4.
The second equation is twice the first.
Eliminating the first column produces a zero row.
There is no pivot in the y column. Choose any real t for y, then solve for x.
Substitution gives 4 in the first equation and 8 in the second for every t.

exercises.prompt: Find x in this system.

solutionSteps.text: Add the left and right sides.
The other variable is y = 3; both equations check.

exercises.prompt: Enter the solution as a 2×1 column matrix. Use rows separated by semicolons.

hints.text: Eliminate x from the second equation.
Subtract three times the first equation.
Solve for y and substitute into the first equation.

exercises.prompt: How many solutions does this system have?

hints.text: Compare twice the first equation with the second.

solutionSteps.text: A contradiction means no pair satisfies both equations.

mistakes: Never multiply a row by zero: that destroys information.
A zero row is not a contradiction; a row with zero coefficients and a nonzero constant is.
summary: Row operations preserve solutions because they are reversible. Pivot columns identify solved variables; missing pivots may produce free variables.

title: Vectors, span & independence
description: See vectors as directions, then discover what they can build.
learningObjectives: Add and scale vectors component by component.
Describe span geometrically.
Recognize independent directions in two dimensions.
bigIdea: A vector records a direction and a size. Starting at the origin, its components tell you how far to move horizontally and vertically. Scaling stretches or reverses that move; addition joins two moves head to tail.

definitions.text: A vector in the plane is a column with two real components.
A linear combination adds scaled vectors.
The span is the set of every linear combination. Independence means only all-zero coefficients produce the zero vector.

reasoning: If one nonzero vector is a multiple of another, both point along one line, so combinations stay on that line. Two nonparallel vectors give two separate directions; their coefficient matrix has a nonzero determinant and reaches every point of the plane.

formulas.text: For two plane vectors, this nonzero determinant tests independence.

steps.text: Start with two vectors.
Add matching components.
Use the horizontal and vertical unit vectors.
Scale the horizontal move by 3 and the vertical move by −2.
Every plane vector (a,b) can be built as ae₁ + be₂, so their span is the whole plane.
Compare the two vectors.
The second is three times the first.
Coefficients 3 and −1 are not both zero, so independence fails. The span is a line, not the whole plane.

exercises.prompt: Enter 2v + w as a column matrix.

hints.text: Scale both components of v by 2.
Add the corresponding components of w.

exercises.prompt: Compute the determinant of the matrix with these columns.

hints.text: Place v and w in separate columns.

exercises.prompt: What is the span of these vectors?

hints.text: Check whether w is a multiple of v.
Every combination becomes a multiple of v.
A single nonzero direction traces a line.

solutionSteps.text: The coefficient can be any real number. The span is the line through v and the origin.

mistakes: A negative scalar reverses direction; it does not change just one component.
Two vectors need not be perpendicular to be independent.
summary: Span asks what can be built; independence asks whether any supplied direction is redundant. A basis is an independent spanning set.

title: Dot products & projection
description: Find the part of a vector pointing in a chosen direction.
learningObjectives: Compute a dot product.
Project onto a nonzero vector.
Verify the residual is perpendicular.
bigIdea: Projection is a vector’s shadow along a direction. It separates a vector into a part along that direction and a leftover perpendicular part. This is the geometric basis of best-fit approximations.

definitions.text: The dot product multiplies matching components and sums them.
Two nonzero vectors are orthogonal when their dot product is zero.
The length of u is the square root of its dot product with itself.

reasoning: Write the shadow as cu for nonzero u. Requiring the leftover v−cu to be perpendicular to u gives (v−cu)·u = 0. Solving for c gives the projection formula. The squared distance to any other point tu on the line is the squared residual plus (c−t)²‖u‖², so the shadow is the closest point.

formulas.text: Projection onto the line generated by nonzero u.
The residual is orthogonal to u.

steps.text: Project v onto the horizontal unit vector.
Compute the scalar coefficient.
Multiply u by 3.
Use an unnormalized direction.
Compute numerator and denominator.
Scale u and compute the residual.
Check perpendicularity.
Remove from w its component along u.
Compute the projection.
Subtract the projection to produce a perpendicular direction.
Normalize each vector by its length √2 to get an orthonormal pair.

exercises.prompt: Compute the dot product.
Enter the projection as a column matrix.
Can you project onto the zero vector using this formula?

hints.text: Compute the zero vector’s squared length.

solutionSteps.text: The line direction is not defined; the formula requires a nonzero u.

mistakes: Divide by u·u, not the length of u.
Projection is a vector; the coefficient alone is a scalar.
summary: Projection chooses the closest point on a line. Subtracting the shadow gives a perpendicular residual.

title: Transformations & eigenvectors
description: Find directions a matrix stretches without turning.
learningObjectives: Apply a matrix to a vector.
Find eigenvalues of a 2×2 matrix.
Check an eigenvector by multiplication.
bigIdea: A matrix transforms every input vector into an output vector. Most directions turn. An eigenvector is a nonzero direction whose output stays on the same line: the eigenvalue tells you the stretch, reversal, or collapse.

definitions.text: A matrix acts on a column vector.
An eigenvector v must be nonzero; λ is its eigenvalue.
The kernel consists of inputs sent to zero; the range consists of all outputs.

reasoning: Rearrange Av = λv to (A−λI)v = 0. A nonzero solution exists only when A−λI is singular. In two dimensions that means its determinant is zero. Solve that scalar equation first, then solve a homogeneous system for each eigenvalue.

steps.text: The matrix scales horizontal and vertical directions separately.
Multiply the horizontal unit vector.
Its eigenvalue is 2. The vertical unit vector similarly has eigenvalue 3.
Form the characteristic determinant.
The roots are 2 and 3. For λ = 3 solve the first row.
Choose x = 1 and check.
Consider a 90-degree rotation.
Compute the characteristic polynomial.
There are no real roots. Every nonzero real vector turns 90 degrees, so no real direction stays on its line. Over complex numbers the eigenvalues are i and −i.

exercises.prompt: What eigenvalue belongs to v?

hints.text: The first component is multiplied by 4.

exercises.prompt: Enter Av as a column matrix.

hints.text: Use each row against the column.

exercises.prompt: Is the zero vector an eigenvector?

hints.text: Read the nonzero condition in the definition.
The equation holds for zero for every λ.
Zero does not select a direction or a particular stretch.

solutionSteps.text: Zero always satisfies the equation but is excluded by definition.
An eigenvector must describe a nonzero direction.

mistakes: Eigenvalues are scalars; eigenvectors are nonzero vectors.
Not every real matrix has a real eigenvector.
summary: Eigenvectors reveal invariant directions of a transformation. Always check Av = λv after solving.

title: Separable equations & growth
description: Connect a rate of change to the quantity that changes.
learningObjectives: Interpret a derivative as a rate.
Separate and integrate an equation.
Use an initial condition and retain equilibrium solutions.
bigIdea: A differential equation relates a changing quantity to its rate of change. If a population grows at a fixed percentage rate, more population means more growth. A separable equation lets us collect all y factors on one side and all x factors on the other.

definitions.text: dy/dx is the instantaneous rate of change of y with respect to x.
A separable equation factors into a function of x times a function of y.
An initial condition selects one curve from a family.

reasoning: Where h(y) is nonzero, divide by h(y) and use the chain rule to integrate. Before dividing, check h(y)=0 separately: those constant solutions can be lost. An integration constant is needed because differentiation removes additive constants.

steps.text: The rate depends only on x.
Integrate both sides.
If y(0) = 3, then C = 3.
Separate for nonzero y; retain y = 0 separately.
Integrate and exponentiate.
Use y(0) = 3.
Check the derivative is 2y and the initial value is 3.
Separate where y is nonzero; y = 0 is also a solution.
Integrate and solve for y.
Apply y(0) = 1.
The maximal interval containing 0 is x < 1. The solution blows up as x approaches 1; it cannot continue through that point.

exercises.prompt: Find C if y(0) = 4.
Find k when the solution satisfies y′ = −3y.

hints.text: Match the rate in the equation.

solutionSteps.text: The specified rate is −3, so k = −3.

exercises.prompt: Which solution is lost if you divide by y?

hints.text: Try a constant y whose derivative is zero.

solutionSteps.text: The zero function has derivative zero.
xy is also zero, so y = 0 is an equilibrium solution.

mistakes: Check equilibrium solutions before dividing by a function of y.
Keep the integration constant and specify intervals when denominators can vanish.
summary: Separate factors, integrate, recover any equilibrium solutions, apply the initial condition, and check the result in the original equation.

title: First-order linear equations
description: Use an integrating factor to turn two terms into one derivative.
learningObjectives: Put an equation in standard form.
Derive and apply an integrating factor.
Check the general solution and an initial value.
bigIdea: The product rule contains two terms: one differentiates the first factor and one differentiates the second. An integrating factor deliberately reshapes a linear equation so its left side becomes exactly that product derivative.

definitions.text: Standard linear form; P and Q depend on x, and y is not squared.
An integrating factor is a nonzero multiplier μ chosen so μ′ = Pμ.

reasoning: Multiplying by μ gives μy′ + μPy. Since μ′=μP, the left side is μy′+μ′y, the derivative of μy. Integrating this derivative leaves a single algebraic step to isolate y. Work on an interval where P and Q are continuous.

steps.text: Identify P = 2 and Q = 6.
Integrate P and exponentiate.
Multiply and recognize the product rule.
Integrate both sides.
Divide by the integrating factor.
Use the general solution of y′ + 2y = 6.
Substitute x = 0.
Differentiate and check.
Work on x > 0 so 1/x is continuous.
Find the integrating factor.
Multiply by x, integrate, and divide.
Check the C terms cancel in y′ + y/x.

exercises.prompt: For μ = eᵏˣ, what is k?

solutionSteps.text: The integrating factor is e⁴ˣ, so k = 4.

exercises.prompt: Find C using the initial condition.
Which equation is linear in y?

hints.text: y and its derivative must occur to the first power.
The coefficient can depend on x.
A y² term makes the equation nonlinear.

solutionSteps.text: A coefficient x multiplying y is allowed.
y′ + xy = x² has standard linear form with P(x) = x and Q(x) = x².

mistakes: Divide by the coefficient of y′ before identifying P.
Do not forget to divide by μ after integrating.
summary: An integrating factor is a product-rule device, not a formula to memorize without meaning. Verify by differentiating the result.

title: Second-order equations & oscillation
description: Connect characteristic roots to growth, decay, and oscillation.
learningObjectives: Use an exponential trial solution.
Handle distinct, repeated, and complex roots.
Apply two initial conditions.
bigIdea: A second-order equation tracks how acceleration relates to position and velocity. With constant coefficients, exponentials are convenient because each derivative only multiplies them by a constant. Complex roots package sine and cosine oscillations into real solutions.

definitions.text: A homogeneous constant-coefficient equation has zero forcing.
Superposition means sums of solutions are solutions for a homogeneous linear equation.
Two initial conditions usually specify position and velocity.

reasoning: Substitute y=eʳˣ; its first and second derivatives are reʳˣ and r²eʳˣ. Dividing by the nonzero exponential gives ar²+br+c=0. Two independent solutions span the solution space. A repeated root needs xeʳˣ as the second solution; complex conjugate roots yield real sine and cosine factors.

steps.text: Form the polynomial.
Factor.
Write the two independent exponentials.
Factor the characteristic equation.
Use the repeated-root form.
Differentiate xe⁻ˣ twice to verify the second solution.
Combine the coefficients: (x−2)+2(1−x)+x=0.
The characteristic roots are ±2i.
Write the real family.
The first condition gives C₁ = 1. Differentiate to use the second.
The selected solution oscillates with angular frequency 2.

exercises.prompt: Give the larger characteristic root.

hints.text: Find two numbers with sum 5 and product 6.

solutionSteps.text: The roots are 2 and 3; the larger is 3.

exercises.prompt: Find C₂.

hints.text: At x = 0, sine is zero and cosine is one.

exercises.prompt: Which is the second independent solution for a repeated root r = −1?

hints.text: Repeating the same exponential does not create independence.
The repeated-root formula introduces a factor x.

solutionSteps.text: The second is xe⁻ˣ; direct substitution confirms it satisfies the equation.

mistakes: Two copies of the same exponential are not independent.
A second-order initial-value problem needs two conditions.
summary: The characteristic roots determine the form of a homogeneous constant-coefficient solution. Substitute to check and use both initial conditions.

title: Euler’s method & slope fields
description: Approximate a solution by following its local direction.
learningObjectives: Read a slope field.
Calculate Euler steps.
Understand approximation error and step-size limits.
bigIdea: At each point a differential equation tells us a direction. Euler’s method follows that direction for a short step, then asks for a new direction. It uses tangent-line approximations, so the computed values generally differ from the exact curve.

definitions.text: A slope field draws small line segments with slope f(x,y).
A step size h is the horizontal distance between approximation points.
The Euler update uses the slope at the beginning of the step.

reasoning: The derivative is the limiting change in y divided by change in x. For a small finite h, approximate the change by hf(x,y). Taylor’s theorem gives a one-step error proportional to h² for a sufficiently smooth solution; over a fixed interval the global error is typically proportional to h. Smaller steps often help, but explicit Euler can still be unstable for stiff equations.

formulas.text: For y′ = ky, the update is a geometric multiplier.

steps.text: Use y′ = y with initial value 1 and h = 0.1.
The starting slope is 1.
This estimates y(0.1); the exact value e⁰·¹ is approximately 1.10517.
Reuse the new value to calculate the next slope.
Step again.
The exact value at 0.2 is approximately 1.22140; the error is about −0.01140.
The exact solution decays for this equation.
Choose an overly large step h = 0.3.
The sequence begins 1, −2, 4, −8 and grows in magnitude. The approximation is unstable although the actual solution decays.
For this negative coefficient stability requires |1−10h| < 1, or 0 < h < 0.2.

exercises.prompt: Compute y₁.
Compute y₂ using two Euler steps.

hints.text: Use the new y value as the next slope.

exercises.prompt: For decay y′ = −10y, is h = 0.3 stable?

hints.text: Magnitude greater than 1 amplifies each step.

solutionSteps.text: The magnitude exceeds 1, so this step size is unstable.

mistakes: Use the new y value for the next slope.
Euler output is an approximation, not an exact solution; label it accordingly.
summary: Euler follows local slopes. Compare with an exact solution when available and inspect both error and stability.
